headline: VOO remains the default; investigate only a few clearly defined alternatives.
subtitle: Deep research is an argument to test, not a signal to buy.
summary: We keep a diversified VOO base. Today we concentrate on a few public-company and commodity exposures, calculating what their historical accounts show, what their market prices assume, and which future evidence should change our view.

assets.name: MARVELL TECHNOLOGY, INC

facts.observation: MRVL recorded annual revenue (sales) of $8.19 billion for the fiscal year ending 2026-01-31. Revenue changed +42.1% relative to the preceding reported year. That is the sales trend, not a statement about how much cash is available. The separate cash-flow statement reports $1.75 billion of cash generated by operating activities. That amount differs from accounting profit because of noncash accounting items and timing differences in payments. After subtracting $354.1 million spent on property and equipment, our simplified free cash flow is $1.40 billion. This is an estimate of cash remaining after those investments, not guaranteed cash available for shareholders or a prediction of future cash flow. Free cash flow was positive in 3 of 3 available annual observations. [S1]
facts.financial_health: The latest available cash balance is $3.93 billion and the SEC long-term debt tag is $4.96 billion. That debt tag is not a measure of every financial obligation. [S1]
facts.valuation: A reverse cash-flow check asks a useful question: what growth would today's price need to justify it? We project from the last reported annual free cash flow using an assumed constant growth rate for five years, then discount those cash flows back to today. Under deliberately fixed assumptions of an 11% required return, 2% perpetual growth beyond year five and no net borrowing, the price implies approximately 78.3% annual free-cash-flow growth over five years. If growth were instead 0% growth → 7% of today's market cap; 5% growth → 9% of today's market cap; 10% growth → 11% of today's market cap. These are sensitivity calculations, not company-specific fair values. [S1][S2]
facts.counter_case: An important alternative explanation is that last year's cash generation may not represent a normal year. Competitive changes, industry cycles and working-capital timing can make a stock look inexpensive right before its profits decline. Our next test is to compare the latest quarterly filing with the prior three annual years.
facts.decision: RESEARCH / WATCH MRVL; no automatic purchase. Demand an independently justified earnings path and a margin of safety before diverting VOO contributions.
facts.next_check: Read the latest 10-Q and management risk discussion; normalize margins and cash conversion across a full business cycle.

assets.name: Physical gold

facts.observation: GLD is an exchange-traded route into physical gold, not a claim of owning the spot commodity directly. Its adjusted share price changed -2.1% over three months and -15.4% over six months. That is -22.4 percentage points versus VOO over those same six months. Price date: 2026-10-23. [S1][S2]
facts.financial_health: Unlike a company, a commodity has no earnings or free cash flow to forecast. Its case depends on economic demand, interest rates, currency conditions and fund costs.
facts.valuation: For this exposure, monitor underlying commodity prices, financing conditions and ETF tracking costs rather than applying a company discounted-cash-flow formula.
facts.counter_case: If interest-bearing assets become relatively more attractive, a commodity without cash distributions can lose demand. Past price momentum alone is not evidence of future outperformance.
facts.decision: DIVERSIFICATION WATCH, not a performance-chasing trade. Compare the benefit of adding this exposure to your existing VOO holdings against extra costs and volatility.
facts.next_check: Compare the fund's issuer documentation, charges and tracking against VOO, then test a modest allocation across different inflation and equity-market regimes.
